headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage from shared filesystem and shell-based handoff between oh-my-openagent and xonsh; cascading errors are also plausible.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: oh-my-openagent can ingest files, AGENTS.md, README.md, and runtime-injected MCP/hook outputs, while xonsh reads and executes shell content from the filesystem/stdin. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path through shared content, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled instructions into a file that agent_b later reads or executes
IF a shared workspace or copied shell script bridges agent_a outputs into agent_b input
mitigations: Restrict both agents to separate working directories
Disable automatic execution of file contents in xonsh sessions
Require manual review before agent_a-generated files are sourced or run
Add provenance labels to agent_a outputs before handoff
requires-engineering: enforce content-type separation between instructions and data

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress and touch sensitive operational data: agent_a handles provider auth prompts and session history, while agent_b reads filesystem contents, configuration, and environment variables. If they share a workspace, either can expose the other's data class through outbound requests. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default-like setups, not provably blocked.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a filesystem or project directory
IF either agent sends local file contents or environment-derived context to a remote service
mitigations: Separate secrets and project files into different directories
Remove provider auth prompts from shared workspaces
Audit outbound requests for file-content inclusion
Use per-agent environment variable scoping
requires-engineering: add egress allowlists and redaction

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b can write the filesystem and execute shell commands, while agent_a can spawn subprocesses and uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. Even though agent_a's write capability is not explicit, both can mutate shared local state through different mechanisms, so conflicts over files or generated artifacts are plausible. Lack of locking makes this a medium-risk overlap.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same writable directory
IF agent_a subprocesses and agent_b shell commands modify the same artifact without locking
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate output directory
Serialize writes with a simple lock file
Avoid concurrent runs on the same project tree
Review generated files before commit or execution
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can produce tool-mediated outputs and agent_b can execute shell commands, so A's output may become B's input without a verification step. That creates a realistic cascade from mistaken or malicious instructions into concrete actions. The pair is not documented as having a built-in validation boundary, so uncertainty favors medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-generated text as shell commands or scripts
IF no human or automated verification step checks agent_a outputs before execution
mitigations: Insert a review step before any execution of agent_a output
Use dry-run mode for shell actions
Log and diff proposed commands before running them
Limit agent_a to advisory output only
requires-engineering: add schema validation for handoff artifacts

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either open-source agent, so a concrete compliance breach is not established. However, agent_a handles provider auth prompts and session history while agent_b reads environment and filesystem contents, so compliance gaps could arise if regulated data is placed in shared local state. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace or environment variables
IF retention or residency requirements apply to files both agents can access
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared directories
Purge session history after use
Separate secret-bearing environments from analysis environments
Document retention expectations for both agents
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing
